b41577cec9.why: The old tell is fixed. The key (no selection of sicker women) is still the only choice about which women went where, but that is the one thing an assignment rule speaks to. The two new lures are the real 9th-grade over-readings of a fair sort: that it removes chance (JLL: only the 42,795 births did that) and that it makes everything but the staff equal (birth position and the priest's walk still differed). Foul air stays as the miasma lure. The stem now says 'went to', so 'was sent' no longer echoes. Facts hold: one in ten (98.4 per 1,000) against under one in twenty-five (36.2 per 1,000); allocation on alternate days; 'by accident rather than design, a controlled trial'; the birth-position and priest-route changes did not move the death rate. Voice is clean.

954aa34231.why: The old echo is fixed: the key no longer says 'cut'. Both strong lures now use a stem detail (the autopsy room's air; the wound), so matching words does not pick the key. The student has to see that the corpse-fouled scalpel, not the room or the prick as such, was the new factor. Fear and shock is weaker but historically honest (Braun's 'emotional traumata'). The date is fixed: sources date only the death (13 March 1847), and the stem now says 'was pricked ... and died in March 1847'. The autopsy findings matched the mothers' (Grokipedia: 'virtually identical'). The context states that the wound was only the way in.

4a90ee9557.why: 'Cadaverous particles' is gone from the stem. Every choice now picks up a stem element (the matter, the death rate, his clinic's deaths, the lime), so no single word echo marks the key. The key is no longer the only non-statistical choice: the lime's smell is non-statistical and plainly showable (Grokipedia: he chose it for removing 'persistent cadaveric odors'). Each lure is something he really could show: 1848 at 1.27 percent, and the earlier years' tables. Facts hold: April 18.3 percent, July 1.2 percent; Klein demanded mechanisms 'beyond mere statistical correlations'; Wikipedia says he 'could not offer a theoretical explanation'. The context now says 'in Vienna', which is true on either account of the asylum.

d7a385bddf.why: The elimination route is closed. All four choices grant that air reached the broth and give the bend a different job, so the stem's 'open at the tip' and Pouchet's oxygen objection no longer knock out lures. Only knowing, or reasoning, that microbes ride on dust decides. 'Dried' and 'cooled' would reopen the Schwann objection (changed air), and neither is true of the moist bend. The 'life force' lure is the honest old vital-force view, and it would not answer Pouchet anyway. In those two choices 'it' reads naturally as the air. Facts hold: Wikipedia says the flask answered Pouchet's claim that 'the oxygen in air was needed for life to arise'; air moves in and out; particles stick to the moist glass of the bend; Grokipedia says it stayed sterile 'even after months'; Pasteur named particles, not the air or a 'vital force'.

32c6088eba.why: The missing result is fixed: the stem now says the control mice were treated 'in the same way' and 'none of them fell ill', so the evidence is on the page. The key is what a control isolates. All three lures are real over-readings of one comparison: rods rather than the rest of the matter (the most tempting, and why Koch went on to pure cultures), a poison rather than a germ, and a cut as the only way in (false: Grokipedia says anthrax is also caught by inhalation and ingestion). None is nonsense, and none is a second answer. Facts hold: the Nobel biography has the home-made wood slivers, the spleens of anthrax dead, all killed, and the healthy-spleen-blood mice inoculated at the same time without disease; National Geographic has the small incision; Koch was district physician in Wollstein 1872-1879.

8fcab60a09.why: The match between 'no sign of the disease' and 'none of the well' is gone, and so is the only two-part choice. The four choices now cross two halves (the step bends or stands; the germ is the cause or not, or the whole method falls), and they are parallel. 'The step stood, so the germ could not be the cause' is the strong strict-rule lure. Reading the stem's 'never fell ill' rules out the incubation rescue, which is legitimate use of evidence, not a tell for the key. Facts hold: Wikipedia has the postulates 'formulated by Robert Koch and Friedrich Loeffler in 1884' and says 'the fourth postulate was added later'. It gives the first step as found in all the sick but 'should not be found in healthy organisms'. It records almost 100 autopsies, the infection found 'in each', and that Koch 'abandoned the universalist requirement of the first postulate when he discovered asymptomatic carriers of cholera'. Grokipedia puts 75-90 percent of cholera infections as mild or asymptomatic.

149b4e6d94.why: Only the dead lure changed. 'Amputate sooner' did not follow from reading Pasteur. 'Keep each wound cold so that it would rot more slowly' is the kitchen idea of slowing spoilage, a live misreading of 'why broth spoils', and it is parallel to the others. It was not Lister's plan: Lister 1867 describes a dressing 'capable of destroying the life of the floating particles'. The question asks what he set out to do, so there is still one answer. The stem, key and card were already verified (16 of 35, 1865, oxygen 'universally regarded as the agent').
